content: Bruxism is a condition characterized by the repetitive, involuntary grinding or clenching of teeth. This behavior can occur during the day (awake bruxism) or at night (sleep bruxism). The term bruxism was first introduced in English by Frohman in 1931, while the French term La Bruxomanie was coined by Marie Pielkiewics in 1907. Bruxism is not a learned habit but rather a reflexive chewing activity. Chewing is a complex neuromuscular process controlled by reflex nerve pathways and higher brain centers. During sleep, the reflex pathways remain active, while higher brain control is diminished, leading to bruxism in some individuals. Although bruxism is often mild and not problematic, it can become severe and symptomatic in certain cases. The etiology of bruxism is multifactorial and can be categorized into psychosocial, peripheral, and pathophysiological factors. Pathophysiological mechanisms involve disturbances in the central neurotransmitter system and imbalances in the direct and indirect pathways of the basal ganglia, which are responsible for coordinating movement. Dopamine-mediated transmission plays a significant role in this imbalance. For example, acute use of dopamine precursors like L-dopa can inhibit bruxism, while chronic use may exacerbate it. Similarly, serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and amphetamines, which influence dopamine levels, have been associated with bruxism. Nicotine, which stimulates dopaminergic activity, may also explain the higher prevalence of bruxism among smokers. Psychosocial factors, such as stress and anxiety, are also implicated in bruxism, although large-scale longitudinal studies are lacking to confirm their definitive role. Additionally, peripheral factors, such as dental occlusion, may contribute to the condition. Bruxism is one of the most common sleep disorders, affecting 30 to 40 million Americans. It occurs equally in men and women and is more prevalent in children under six years of age, with incidence decreasing with age. Risk factors for bruxism include obstructive sleep apnea, alcohol consumption, caffeine intake, smoking, and anxiety. The symptoms of bruxism often begin in childhood, coinciding with the eruption of primary teeth, and may persist into adulthood if risk factors remain. While bruxism typically follows a benign course, untreated cases can lead to complications such as tooth wear, hypersensitivity, mobility, temporomandibular joint (TMJ) pain, jaw muscle tenderness, temporal headaches, and poor sleep quality. Other signs include tongue indentations, the presence of a linea alba along the buccal mucosa, and gingival recession. Severe cases may result in dental fractures, soft tissue injuries, difficulty chewing, and head and neck pain. Diagnosis of bruxism is primarily clinical, based on a history of tooth grinding during sleep, often reported by bed partners. Common symptoms include involuntary rhythmic contractions of the masticatory muscles during sleep, morning headaches, jaw pain, TMJ clicking, and dental deformities such as thermal sensitivity, hypermobility, and tooth wear. Severe cases may present with soft tissue injuries, dental fractures, and TMJ dysfunction. Management of bruxism begins with the removal of any offending agents, such as medications or substances contributing to the condition. A wait-and-see approach is often recommended for medication-induced bruxism, as symptoms may resolve with the cessation of the offending agent. Pharmacological treatment focuses on symptom relief, with buspirone (15-20 mg/day) and gabapentin (100-300 mg/day) being commonly prescribed. Surgical intervention is considered the mainstay of treatment for severe cases of bruxism, particularly when complications arise. Indications for surgery include mechanical wear of teeth, hypersensitivity, tooth fractures, loss of periodontal support, failure of dental restorations or implants, hypertrophy of masticatory muscles, jaw muscle tenderness, limited mouth opening, and TMJ pain.
